newsitem.title: DENMARK: NATO's Solana says no would-be members ruled out.
newsitem.headline: NATO's Solana says no would-be members ruled out.

text.p: NATO Secretary- General Javier Solana on Thursday followed the United States in seeking to reassure the three Baltic states that they had not been ruled out as candidates for alliance membership.

Speaking at the culmination of a 13-nation naval exercise by NATO, non-aligned and former Warsaw Pact vessels, Solana appeared to seek to play down the widespread expectation that NATO has already relegated Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia to the back of the queue.

"At this very moment NATO is going through a process of dialogue with all the parties who have shown a wish to join NATO. That process will end probably at the end of December, we will make an assessment at that moment."

"I want to say very clearly now that no country is ruled out and no country is ruled in. We are talking to everybody and we will try to take a decision at the right moment, probably not before the middle of 1997," he added.

In a letter to Baltic defence ministers made public on Wednesday U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said that remarks he made last month seen as ruling out early Baltic NATO membership had been misinterpreted.
"I believe that the Balts are fully eligible for NATO membership," he wrote.
The Baltic states, who won their independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, are nervous of their large and volatile Russian neighbour and anxious to obtain the security mantle of NATO membership.

Russian leaders have hitherto passionately opposed NATO expansion on its borders as a security threat, but on a visit to NATO headquarters in Belgium this week Russian security chief Alexander Lebed softened the tone considerably.
Lebed told his former Cold War foes that while he would prefer not to see the alliance expand eastward it had the right to do so and Russia should not react hysterically.

Solana was asked if reports from Moscow of a backlash of conservative anger at Lebed's conciliatory tone gave rise to concern that NATO might have gained a friend at the expense of Lebed's political standing at home.
"I doubt it, I hope that I have a new friend and without any doubt he is a politician, you can believe me," Solana said.
Solana made a point of sending wishes for President Boris Yeltsin's recovery from an impending heart operation.
"I do very much hope that President Yeltsin will recover from his operation and will continue his mandate," he said.

The 15-day Baltic sea manoeuvres, named Co-Operative Venture 96, constitute the largst single naval exercise yet held by NATO's Partnership for Peace, bringing together 26 ships from Britain, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Sweden, and the United States.
The objective is to practise together blockade, mine clearing and other operations that might be demanded of a future multinational peacekeeping force.
A NATO officer said that Russia had been invited to participate in the exercise but had declined, saying it was too busy preparing for the 300th anniversary of the Russian navy.
